# The benchmark: baselines, datasets and the rules {#sec-baselines}

*Before this chapter:* @sec-isla (tokens, slices, measure weights, global directions and scalars), @sec-metrics (the
area-weighted relative L2 error) and @sec-invariances (the three scorings: native mesh, uniform point cloud, rotated and
translated).

**ISLA is measured against two public slice-attention transformers, GeoTransolver and Transolver, on eight datasets and
nine tasks. The protocol fixes everything except the architecture, and every number in the book is scored by it.** The
baselines are the public model classes, run unmodified from the PhysicsNeMo recipe. Each architecture is scored at one
reference configuration, chosen once on two selection datasets (@sec-selection). This chapter says what each baseline computes and what it is given, states
the rules of the comparison and how the reference configurations were chosen, shows every dataset on one page, and defines
how a checkpoint is scored. It closes by defining the tag that marks a study run on another configuration of ISLA.

```{python}
#| label: setup-baselines
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import standing as S
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
FR = J("char/ref80_frontier_2026-10-02.json")["candidates"]
SEL = J("char/ref80_select_2026-10-03.json")
REF = {"ISLA": "isla_w512_s512", "GeoTransolver": "gt_h256", "Transolver": "t_h512_l16_c100k"}
```

## The baselines and what each one sees {#sec-part-baseline}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver share ISLA's core mechanism, routing points into a few hundred soft slices, and differ in
what they are given: coordinates in the dataset's frame and the freestream vector as a raw feature.** Transolver (Wu et
al., ICML 2024, arXiv [2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) introduced *physics attention*. Each layer assigns
every point a softmax mixture over $M$ slices, pools the point features into one token per slice, lets the $M$ slice tokens
attend to one another, and scatters the result back to the points through the same mixture. In the language of
@sec-landscape, physics attention is a low-rank factorization of an $N \times N$ attention kernel through a learned soft
partition: a restriction from $N$ points to $M$ slices, a dense operator on the slices, and a prolongation back. The cost is
$O(NM)$ instead of $O(N^2)$. GeoTransolver adds a geometry encoder and a context projector that condition every layer on the
geometry and on the global inputs. ISLA keeps the factorization and changes what enters it (@fig-family-diagram).

```{mermaid}

%%|   boundary tokens from them, consumes their positions, normals and measure weights only through invariants, and reads
%%|   each global direction as a unit vector. How to read this: the diagram shows inputs and structure
%%|   on the surface tasks, not accuracy; the interior inputs are in @tbl-model-inputs.
flowchart TB

        B2["GeoTransolver only: geometry encoder,<br/>context projector"]:::learned
        B3["physics attention × layers:<br/>softmax routing of points into slices,<br/>attention among slices, scatter back"]:::learned
        B4["linear head: every output channel"]:::learned
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4
    end
    subgraph I["ISLA"]
        direction LR
        I1["one full-resolution mesh per named boundary condition<br/>per cell: position, unit normal, measure weight<br/>global: unit direction(s), scalars"]:::data
        I2["length unit L and declared scales;<br/>boundary-token draw; invariant seed"]:::fixed
        I3["slice layers × 12:<br/>measure-weighted routing, anchors,<br/>relational invariants, read-back"]:::learned
        I4["heads: learned invariant coefficients<br/>× a basis that rotates with the body"]:::learned
        I1 --> I2 --> I3 --> I4
```

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's default surface model. Per surface point it receives a six-channel feature, the point's
coordinates (centered on the case) and its unit normal. Its geometry encoder reads the coordinates a second time, and its
context projector reads the global vector. On the surface tasks its ball-query local-feature path is off, as in the
recipe's shipped configuration. On the DrivAerML Volume task the recipe's volume configuration turns it on; that model is
*GeoTransolver-volume*. A rotated car is a different input to it, because it reads coordinates (@sec-pose).

::: {#sec-transolver}
**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder and the context projector. Per point it receives the
coordinates and the normal, and the global vector is concatenated to every point's features.
:::

**ISLA** receives one full-resolution boundary mesh per named boundary condition, from which it reads each cell's position,
unit normal and measure weight, and each global direction as a unit vector. It reads positions only through differences to
its anchors (@sec-isla). On the interior tasks the prediction points join as tokens, and each one reads its exact distance and
direction to the boundary meshes (@sec-exact-geometry-draw).

@tbl-architectures gives the three reference configurations side by side, with the parameter count and the training memory
the selection read. @tbl-model-inputs lists, per dataset, what each model's forward call receives; the dataset chapters point to it.

```{python}
#| label: cell-tbl-architectures
#| output: asis
rows = [("ISLA", "12", "512", "512", "8", "200,000", "3.75e-4"),
        ("GeoTransolver", "12", "256", "256", "8", "200,000", "1e-3"),
        ("Transolver", "16", "512", "256", "8", "100,000", "1e-3")]
out = "| architecture | layers | width | slices | heads | training cells | learning rate | parameters | training peak [GiB] |\n|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|\n"
for a, l, w, m, h, c, lr in rows:
    fc = FR[REF[a]]
    out += f"| {a} | {l} | {w} | {m} | {h} | {c} | {lr} | {fc['n_parameters'] / 1e6:.1f}M | {fc['train_peak_gib']:.0f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": The three reference configurations. *Slices*: $M$, the number of soft slices per layer. *Heads*: attention heads "
      "among the slice tokens. *Parameters* and *training peak* are measured on the DrivAerML Surface task in the one-epoch training runs "
      "that fixed the memory frontier of the selection (peak device memory of a training epoch, maximum over four GPUs, batch "
      "one, bfloat16); they change by task with the input and output channels. How to read this: the table states what each "
      "model is, not how accurate it is; the three are matched on the memory budget, not on parameters or cells. Sources: the "
      "training-run configurations under results/campaigns_2026-10-02/char/, results/char/ref80_frontier_2026-10-02.json. "
      "{#tbl-architectures}")
```

### Global directions as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars {#sec-unit-direction-rule}

**A problem's global conditions enter ISLA in one form: directions as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars. ISLA enforces
the rule by construction, and every standing's baselines read their global conditions in the same form: the unit direction
alone on HiLiftAeroML, the DrivAerML tasks and SHIFT-SUV, and on AirfRANS the unit direction and the inlet speed
standardized over the training airfoils.** A direction carries no
scale. Whatever scale a pipeline attaches to it, the units the solver ran in, is an accident of the dataset, and a model
would have to learn to ignore it. A magnitude that matters physically, a far-field speed or a Reynolds number, is a scalar
with its own place in the input. ISLA normalizes every global vector it receives and takes magnitudes only as global
scalars (@sec-isla-inputs).

GeoTransolver and Transolver consume whatever vector the pipeline hands them. In the recipe's configurations of the two
models that vector is `U_inf`, in solver units; on HiLiftAeroML it carries the angle of attack, in inches per second, at a
magnitude of 2,680. The standing's baselines are trained with one override that hands them `U_inf_dir` in its place, and on
AirfRANS the standardized inlet speed beside it, the information ISLA reads, at a scale of one (@tbl-model-inputs). The
scale matters before training: GeoTransolver's context projector applies linear maps and a slice softmax to the raw vector,
so its conditioning depends on the magnitude (@tbl-projector).

```{python}
#| label: para-constant-drive
#| output: asis
UDC = S.unit_drive_control(); UDI = S.unit_drive_control("isla")
CD = ("drivaerml_surface", "drivaerml_volume", "shift_suv")   # the datasets whose freestream is one constant vector
UDR = {b: [v for k in CD for v in S.unit_drive(k, b).values()] for b in S.BASELINES}   # unit ÷ physical vector, native, headline fields
print("On the DrivAerML tasks and on SHIFT-SUV every case has the same freestream, so `U_inf` is one constant vector per "
      "dataset and holds no case information. Its scale still reaches the trained model. Retrained reading `U_inf_dir` in place of "
      f"`U_inf`, each baseline at its reference configuration, GeoTransolver's native error moves by at most "
      f"{S.fmt_pct(max(UDR['GeoTransolver'], key=lambda v: abs(v - 1)))} on the headline fields of the three tasks, and Transolver's falls "
      f"by {S.fmt_pct(max(UDR['Transolver']))} to {S.fmt_pct(min(UDR['Transolver']))}, seed means, each against its "
      "physical-vector twin. For Transolver on the DrivAerML Surface task this was registered as a control before it ran: on each arm's "
      f"own draw of 100,000 cells it scores {UDC['pressure_l2']:.3f} times its physical-vector error on pressure and {UDC['wss_l2']:.3f} "
      "times it on wall shear, so the registered band of ±3% holds on wall shear and not on pressure; on the 200,000 cells of ISLA's "
      f"scored set it reads {UDI['pressure_l2']:.3f} and {UDI['wss_l2']:.3f}. The standing's baselines are the unit-direction "
      "checkpoints, and each physical-vector twin stays in its standing artifact as a record. Data: "
      "results/campaigns_2026-10-19/drive_fix/drivefix_scores_2026-10-19.json (the band: PREREG.md beside it), "
```

## The fair-comparison rules {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in the book is produced under the rules below, and a comparison that breaks one is not
reported as a standing.** They fall into three groups: what each model is given, how much training it gets, and how a
difference is read.

**Inputs.**

1. Every model is given the same physical problem: the same cases, the same targets, the same validation and test cases,
   drawn with the same random seed. The inputs differ only as @tbl-model-inputs states. Where a dataset's own rule
   restricts the inputs, it binds as well. AeroZoo's rule admits only the data of the PDE: the boundary meshes with the
   condition type each names, the values prescribed on them and the kinematic viscosity, with the density only to
   convert pressure and shear to pascals. Every other global datum is a label, among them the reference length, speed
   and direction and any Reynolds number built on them. On AeroZoo every model reads only those data, in physical units,
   and a model that wants a length, a velocity scale or a Reynolds number computes it from them (@sec-aerozoo-allowed).
   On every other dataset a reference length,
   where one is used, is one constant for the whole set.
2. No reference configuration trains with augmentation. The rotation-augmented baselines of @sec-pose-contract are a labeled
   control.
3. Boundary conditions enter ISLA as per-cell fields on boundary meshes. GeoTransolver and Transolver have no
   boundary-token path; they receive what their recipe configurations give them, which @tbl-model-inputs lists per
   dataset. On the lug GeoTransolver reads the surface triangles with ISLA's four boundary-condition labels as its geometry
   context, and Transolver reads no boundary label: the loaded and clamped faces are known to it only through the shape
   (@sec-data-conventions).

**Budget.**

4. One recipe trains every model: the same optimizer (Muon on the weight matrices, AdamW on every other parameter), batch
   one, a Huber loss, weight decay $10^{-4}$, bfloat16 autocast, and 500 epochs with the learning rate divided by ten every
   100 epochs. DeepJEB++ trains 40 epochs and AeroZoo 250, for every architecture alike.
5. Each architecture trains at its reference configuration's learning rate on every dataset, with no per-dataset tuning:
   ISLA at $3.75 \times 10^{-4}$, GeoTransolver and Transolver at $10^{-3}$ (@sec-lr-protocol).
6. The configurations are matched on one resource, the 80 GiB training memory per GPU under which they were selected
   (@sec-resource-matching). They differ in parameters and training cells, and @tbl-architectures says by how much.

**Reading.**

7. Every number is scored by one protocol (@sec-protocol): float32, final checkpoints, the same cells per case for every
   architecture, and ISLA's function as its eager path computes it.
8. Two random seeds per configuration (four for ISLA on Tensile2d), all reported. One model *leads* another on a field only when every seed of the
   one lies below every seed of the other and the seed means differ by at least 3%; otherwise the two are *level*.
9. A ratio is always baseline ÷ ISLA, so a value above one favors ISLA.
10. A sealed test split is evaluated once per checkpoint, with the checkpoint and configuration declared beforehand
    (@sec-splits).
11. Every experiment states, in readout units and before it runs, the value that confirms it and the value that refutes it.

### One scoring set per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

**Every number in a family of comparisons is read from one fixed scoring set, and a control that changes it is reported as
a control.** The *scoring set* of a dataset is its fixed validation or test set and its scoring configuration:
on the DrivAerML Surface task, surface pressure and wall shear on 48 held-out cars at 200,000 cells, in float32; on the
DrivAerML Volume task, pressure, velocity and eddy viscosity at 200,000 interior points of the same 48 cars; on
HiLiftAeroML, 180 held-out wing cases shared by every *rung*, a training-set size of a data-efficiency ladder (the
510-case rung trains on 510 cases). A scoring set is never widened after a result is read from it. A control that changes it (another cell count, a pose, a sampling law) is reported as such and never mixed into a
standing. Its limits bind where stated: 48 cars is a small validation set, and two seeds a thin noise estimate
(@sec-limits).

### Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**The reference configurations are matched on the training memory they were selected under, and on nothing else.** They
differ in parameters, training cells and step time. A comparison states those on both sides, or says in the same sentence
where they differ and whether the difference could buy accuracy. Each dataset chapter states them beside its standing. The
memory budget binds on the two selection datasets only. On the DrivAerML Volume task, whose three output fields and interior
prediction points cost more, ISLA and GeoTransolver-volume train above it, and the chapter reports the measured peak as
the configuration's cost there.

### Learning rate {#sec-lr-protocol}

**Every reference configuration trains at one learning rate on every dataset: ISLA at $3.75 \times 10^{-4}$,
GeoTransolver and Transolver at $10^{-3}$.** ISLA's rate is its width rule, $10^{-3} \times 192 / \text{width}$, at width
512. The baselines' rate is set on the command line of every training run of the standings. The recipe's own default,
$3 \times 10^{-3}$ in `conf/train.yaml`, is not used for any of them; some studies train a baseline at it and say so where
they appear.

```{python}
#| label: para-lr-gt
#| output: asis
P3 = J("p200k_trio_reduction_2026-09-19.json")["arms"]
g1, g3 = P3["gt_unit_lr1e3"]["pressure_mean"], P3["gt_unit_lr3e3"]["pressure_mean"]
print(f"GeoTransolver at width 256 on the DrivAerML Surface task, fed the unit direction, scores {g3:.4f} at $3 \\times "
      f"10^{{-3}}$ against {g1:.4f} at $10^{{-3}}$ (surface pressure, 435 training cars, 200,000 cells, seed means; "
      f"results/p200k_trio_reduction_2026-09-19.json), a gap of {100 * (g1 / g3 - 1):.1f}%, inside the 3% band within which "
      "the seed rule calls two models level.")
```


### How the reference configurations were chosen {#sec-selection}

**Each reference configuration was chosen once, among candidates that train under 80 GiB per GPU, on two selection
datasets: the DrivAerML Surface task and HiLiftAeroML at 510 training cases. The registered rule names a winner per
dataset, and the two datasets named different winners for every architecture.** Every candidate trained for 500 epochs on
two seeds and was scored on the native mesh at 200,000 cells, by its seed-mean surface pressure error. The rule, written
before the candidates were scored, takes on each dataset the candidate with the lowest error, with candidates within 3% of
the best counted as tied and the tie going to the one with the lower training peak memory. A candidate that wins on both
datasets is the reference configuration; if the datasets disagree, both winners are listed and the decision is recorded
with its reason.

```{python}
#| label: cell-tbl-selection-winners
#| output: asis
D = SEL["datasets"]
nm = lambda k: "w384_s256" if k == "isla_ref" else k.replace("isla_", "").replace("gt_", "").replace("t_", "")
out = "| architecture | winner on DrivAerML Surface | winner on the 510 wing cases | the two agree | reference configuration |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n"
for arch in S.ARCHS:
    w = SEL["reference"][arch]
    out += (f"| {arch} | {nm(w['winners']['drivaer_surface'])} | {nm(w['winners']['hilift_210'])} | "
            f"{'yes' if w['agreed'] else 'no'} | {nm(REF[arch])} |\n")
print(out)
print(": The registered selection rule, applied per dataset (lowest seed-mean pressure error, ties within 3% to the lower "
      "training peak memory), and the configuration taken. Candidate names as in @tbl-selection. How to read this: the "
      "rule by itself names no reference configuration for any architecture; the last column is the decision described "
      "below. Data: results/char/ref80_select_2026-10-03.json. {#tbl-selection-winners}")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-selection-decision
#| output: asis
def joint(arch):
    cd, cw = D["drivaer_surface"][arch]["candidates"], D["hilift_210"][arch]["candidates"]
    bd = min(v["pressure_l2"] for v in cd.values()); bw = min(v["pressure_l2"] for v in cw.values())
    return {k: (cd[k]["pressure_l2"] / bd, cw[k]["pressure_l2"] / bw, cd[k]["peak_memory_gib"]) for k in cd if k in cw}
JS = {a: joint(a) for a in S.ARCHS}
mj = lambda r: (r[0] + r[1]) / 2
for a in S.ARCHS:   # the decision is the smallest joint score, and also the smallest worse-of-two ratio
    assert min(JS[a], key=lambda k: mj(JS[a][k])) == REF[a] and min(JS[a], key=lambda k: max(JS[a][k][:2])) == REF[a]
def cheaper_ties(a):
    r0 = JS[a][REF[a]]
    return [(k, r) for k, r in JS[a].items() if k != REF[a] and mj(r) <= mj(r0) * 1.03 and r[2] < r0[2]]
pct = lambda x: f"{100 * (x - 1):.1f}%"
gt = JS["GeoTransolver"][REF["GeoTransolver"]]
def best_on(ds, a):
    c = D[ds][a]["candidates"]; return min(c, key=lambda k: c[k]["pressure_l2"])
err = lambda ds, a, k: D[ds][a]["candidates"][k]["pressure_l2"]
def car_best_text(a):
    k = best_on("drivaer_surface", a)
    return (f"{a}'s {nm(k)} scores {err('drivaer_surface', a, k):.4f} on the cars against {err('drivaer_surface', a, REF[a]):.4f} "
            f"for the reference {nm(REF[a])}, and {err('hilift_210', a, k):.4f} on the wings against {err('hilift_210', a, REF[a]):.4f}")
cheapest = [(a, min(cheaper_ties(a), key=lambda kr: kr[1][2])) for a in S.ARCHS if cheaper_ties(a)]
cheap_txt = [f"{nm(k)} ({r[2]:.0f} GiB) for {a}" for a, (k, r) in cheapest]
assert all(best_on("drivaer_surface", a) != REF[a] for a in S.ARCHS)
print("The registered rule named no reference configuration, so the picks were made after the scores were read, by a joint "
      "score: a candidate's error divided by the best candidate's error on each dataset, averaged over the two. Each reference "
      "configuration has the smallest joint score of its architecture, and it is also the candidate that trails the best by the "
      "least on its worse dataset. "
      + ("No tie band was applied to the joint score; had the rule's 3% band been applied to it, with the tie going to the lower "
         "training peak memory, the cheaper " + " and ".join(cheap_txt) + " would have been taken. ")
      + "The joint score did not take the candidate most accurate on the DrivAerML Surface task for any architecture, under the "
      "same budget: " + "; ".join(car_best_text(a) for a in S.ARCHS) + ". "
      f"No GeoTransolver candidate is within 3% of the best on both datasets; width 256 is the best on the wings and trails by "
      f"{pct(gt[0])} on the cars. In the selection's wing runs GeoTransolver and Transolver read the freestream in inch/s (@tbl-hilift-unit-drive), "
      "so the wing scores that decided their picks are scores under that input; a reselection with the unit direction on the wings "
      "is an open question (@sec-oq-reference-selection). @tbl-selection lists every candidate.")
```

```{python}
#| label: cell-tbl-selection
#| output: asis
out = "| architecture | candidate | DrivAerML Surface: error ÷ best | 510 wing cases: error ÷ best | mean | training peak [GiB] |\n|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|\n"
for arch in S.ARCHS:
    rows = sorted(((mj(r), k, r[0], r[1], r[2]) for k, r in JS[arch].items()))
    for j, (m, k, rd, rw, gib) in enumerate(rows):
        lab = f"**{nm(k)} (reference)**" if k == REF[arch] else nm(k)
        out += f"| {arch if j == 0 else ''} | {lab} | {rd:.3f} | {rw:.3f} | {m:.3f} | {gib:.0f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Every candidate of the selection, by architecture: its seed-mean surface pressure error on each selection dataset "
      "divided by the best candidate's on that dataset, the mean of the two (the joint score), and its training peak "
      "memory. Candidate names: `w` width, `s` slices, `d` layers, `h` width of a baseline, `l` its layers, `c100k` trained "
      "at 100,000 cells; an ISLA name lists only what differs from width 384, 256 slices and 12 layers (`w384_s256` is that configuration). How to read this: 1.000 is the best candidate on that "
      "dataset; the table selects configurations and ranks nothing across architectures. Data: "
      "results/char/ref80_select_2026-10-03.json. {#tbl-selection}")
```

## The datasets {#sec-datasets}

**Eight datasets carry the evidence, and all eight supply one input schema: boundary cells with positions, outward
normals and measures, the problem's global conditions, and per-cell boundary data where the problem has them.** One model
implementation therefore runs on all of them. The aerodynamic datasets are external flows with one global direction, the
flow direction ($K = 1$). The solids and brackets exercise the global scalars, the per-cell boundary data and, on the lug and
Tensile2d, the case with no global direction ($K = 0$). @tbl-datasets is the roster and @fig-datasets shows one case of each.

### Datasets beyond external aerodynamics {#sec-datasets-beyond-aero}

**ISLA is written for any steady boundary-driven PDE, and external aerodynamics is its benchmark instance, not its scope.**
Tensile2d, the lug and DeepJEB++ are steady solid-mechanics problems whose loads and boundary conditions vary per case. They
exercise what the aerodynamic datasets leave unused: global scalars, per-cell boundary labels and values, a tensor output,
and problems with no global direction. Every dataset enters the evidence only with GeoTransolver and Transolver trained on
it under the rules above, and with a preregistration written before its first training run. What the set does not cover is stated
in @sec-limits.

### Conventions shared by every dataset {#sec-data-conventions}

**A converted case is one `DomainMesh` file (`.pdmsh`): an `interior` point cloud, one or more named `boundaries`, and a
`global_data` dictionary.** The datasets differ in which of these a model reads and in what the boundary cells carry.

- **Two reader layouts.** The *surface* datasets (the DrivAerML Surface task, HiLiftAeroML, SHIFT-SUV, DeepJEB++) read only
  the boundary mesh. The reader merges the parent file's `global_data` onto it (`MeshReaderWithGlobalData`), and the
  terminal transform `MeshToDomainMesh` places the prediction points at the cell centroids. The *interior* datasets (the
  DrivAerML Volume task, AirfRANS, AeroZoo, Tensile2d, the lug) read the whole `DomainMesh` (`DomainMeshReader`): the
  interior points are the prediction points, and the boundary is kept whole whenever the cell budget exceeds its size.
- **Signed distance is positive outside the solid.** Interior nodes of a solid carry `sdf` $\le 0$, fluid points outside a
  body carry `sdf` $> 0$, and `sdf_normals` is the gradient of that field. Converters negate a source that stores the
  opposite sign.
- **Boundary conditions are per-cell fields.** Each labeled region is a 0/1 indicator on the boundary cells (`bc_fixed`,
  `bc_loaded`, …), and each prescribed value is a field on the cells it applies to and zero elsewhere (`bc_pressure`,
  `bc_load`, …). A prescribed vector enters ISLA as a rank-1 boundary field; one stored component by component is stacked
  into one vector first, because components fed as separate scalars would make the model depend on the dataset's axes. Where a dataset configuration gives
  GeoTransolver and Transolver boundary labels, it writes them as nodal indicators on the interior points
  (@tbl-model-inputs).
- **Global vectors must be data of the problem.** For external aerodynamics `ComputeFreestreamDirection` writes `U_inf_dir`
  from the stored velocity. For a loaded solid the load direction is the global vector. Where the targets are components in
  a fixed frame, ISLA predicts the tensor and the components are read off it (@sec-isla-heads). The dataset's axes are never
  supplied as global vectors (@sec-pose-inputs).
- **Normalization statistics come from the manifest.** Every converter writes `manifest.json` beside the files, with the
  named split lists and per-field means and standard deviations pooled over the training split. A vector target uses one
  isotropic standard deviation, so no component is rescaled per axis.

| dataset | converter | dataset configuration | ISLA configuration |
|---|---|---|---|
| DrivAerML (Surface, Volume) | native files of the dataset release | `datasets/drivaer_ml_surface.yaml`, `drivaer_ml_volume_reference.yaml` | `conf/model/isla_surface.yaml`, `isla_volume.yaml` |
| HiLiftAeroML | native files | `datasets/highlift_surface.yaml` | `conf/model/isla_surface_highlift.yaml` |
| SHIFT-SUV | native files | `datasets/shift_suv_surface.yaml` and the two family files | `conf/model/isla_surface.yaml` |
| AirfRANS | `results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/airfrans_convert.py` | `datasets/airfrans_uvolume_2d.yaml` (ISLA), `airfrans_uvolume.yaml` (the baselines) | `conf/model/isla_volume_airfrans.yaml` |
| AeroZoo | native files of the dataset release | `datasets/aerozoo_uvolume.yaml` and its six held-out-split files, which hold the benchmark protocol's physical PDE inputs only (@sec-data-aerozoo) | `conf/model/isla_volume_aerozoo.yaml` |
| PLAID Tensile2d | `results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/plaid_tensile2d_convert.py` | `results/campaigns_2026-10-02/char/datasets/plaid_tensile2d.yaml` | `conf/model/isla_tensile2d.yaml` |
| GINOT Bracket Lug | `results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/ginot_lug_convert.py` | `results/campaigns_2026-10-02/char/datasets/ginot_lug_volume.yaml` | `conf/model/isla_lug.yaml` |
| DeepJEB++ | `results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/deepjebpp_convert.py` | `results/campaigns_2026-10-02/char/datasets/deepjebpp_surface.yaml` | `conf/model/isla_surface_deepjebpp.yaml` |

: Where each dataset's conversion and configuration live. `datasets/` and `conf/` are relative to the recipe root,
`examples/cfd/external_aerodynamics/unified_external_aero_recipe`. The GeoTransolver and Transolver configurations sit
beside ISLA's in `conf/model/`, with the prefixes `geotransolver_` and `transolver_`. How to read this: the table locates
files; it says nothing about what a model receives, which is @tbl-model-inputs. {#tbl-data-files}

### Splits {#sec-splits}

**Every split in the book is either the dataset's curated manifest used unchanged or a fixed-seed permutation recorded in
the manifest, and a sealed test split is evaluated once per checkpoint.** Where a dataset publishes splits (HiLiftAeroML,
AirfRANS, SHIFT-SUV, PLAID's official ladder), they are used unchanged. Where a split has to be carved out, the draw is a
fixed-seed permutation recorded in the manifest, and every smaller training rung is a prefix of the larger one, so a rung
differs from the next only by the cases it lacks. DrivAerML has one validation set of 48 cars, shared by the Surface and
Volume tasks and by every experiment, with 435 training cars or a nested rung of 27, 54, 109 or 218. HiLiftAeroML's
manifests each hold out one question and overlap, so a test split there is sealed per checkpoint, not once for every experiment. Each
dataset chapter gives its splits in full.

## The scoring protocol {#sec-protocol}

**Every standing scores the final checkpoint of each seed in float32 on 200,000 sampled cells per case, as the area-weighted
relative L2 error averaged over cases, and scores it three ways; AeroZoo is scored on the native mesh only.** @tbl-protocol
gives the settings. The metric is the
area-weighted relative L2 error of @sec-metrics, computed per case and averaged over the cases with equal weight.

| item | setting |
|---|---|
| cells per case at scoring | 200,000 sampled cells, the same for every architecture; a mesh smaller than that is scored whole (the lug, Tensile2d, DeepJEB++, the AirfRANS airfoil); 100,000 interior points on AirfRANS |
| cells per case in training | ISLA and GeoTransolver 200,000 and Transolver 100,000 (its reference configuration) on the DrivAerML tasks, HiLiftAeroML and SHIFT-SUV; every architecture alike on the other tasks: 200,000 on DeepJEB++, 100,000 on AirfRANS, 20,000 on the lug and Tensile2d |
| precision | bfloat16 autocast in training, float32 at scoring |
| ISLA's compiled path | in training, each slice block compiled on its own (`model.compile_blocks=true`) on every dataset but Tensile2d, whose standing trains eagerly. On AirfRANS and the lug, where the compiled blocks compute another function unless Inductor's mix-order reduction is off (@sec-using-cost), the rows shown trained with it off, and their eagerly trained standing is in flight (@sec-standing-table); on the other datasets the geometry runs in the fused kernel, which that fault does not reach. Scoring runs fully eager (`compile=false model.compile_blocks=false`) on AirfRANS, Tensile2d and the lug and keeps the compiled blocks elsewhere |
| checkpoint | the final epoch of each seed; no selection on validation error |
| seeds | 42 and 43, both reported (42 to 45 for ISLA on Tensile2d); the standing quotes the seed mean and applies the seed rule of @sec-fair-comparison |
| metric | area-weighted relative L2 per case, averaged over the scored cases (@sec-metrics) |
| scorings | the *native mesh*; the *uniform point cloud*, the area-proportional law with exact Horvitz–Thompson weights; *rotated and translated*, a random rotation and a translation of one RMS radius per case (the root-mean-square distance of the case's points from their centroid; in-plane on the planar datasets) |
| AeroZoo | the native mesh only, 200,000 interior points of each split's test cases, the relative L2 error per field and case in physical units averaged over cases, the checkpoint of epoch 250 (@sec-aerozoo-allowed) |

: The scoring protocol of every standing. How to read this: the three scorings rescore one checkpoint and train nothing; a
number outside this protocol says so in its caption. {#tbl-protocol}

**The uniform point cloud resamples the scored set only where the scored mesh is larger than the budget.** The protocol
replaces the native subsample of every sub-mesh with an area-proportional draw. A sub-mesh with no more cells than the
budget is returned unchanged, and a point cloud has no cells to draw from. The protocol therefore measures three different
things:

- on the DrivAerML Surface task, HiLiftAeroML and SHIFT-SUV, whose surfaces hold millions of cells, it resamples the scored
  cells for every architecture;
- on the DrivAerML Volume task it changes no model's input: the scored interior points are a point cloud, ISLA reads the
  whole vehicle surface and draws its boundary tokens by area itself, and the baselines do not load the boundary, so the
  column is not applicable; what exact re-meshing of that boundary, and a watertight surface in place of the CFD wall, do
  to ISLA is measured in @sec-interior-boundary-law;
- on AirfRANS, Tensile2d, the lug and DeepJEB++ it returns the native mesh, and the column repeats the native error.

Only the first group appears as a point-cloud standing (@fig-contract-shifts).

::: {.callout-warning title="What the validation set is used for"}
The DrivAerML and HiLiftAeroML accuracy figures are validation-set figures with no checkpoint selection behind them. The
same validation sets selected the reference configurations (@tbl-selection) and were in view when the ablations were
designed, so they are not an untouched test. The sealed HiLiftAeroML test splits were scored once, on regime
extrapolation, with an ISLA study configuration against baselines that read the physical freestream (@sec-hilift); no
reference configuration is scored on them. Because those test sets cover every geometry, the remaining test manifests
are held out per checkpoint but do not confirm a result across the whole set of experiments (@sec-limits).
:::

## The nearest-token form {#sec-checkpoint-form}

**Some figures of trained ISLA (renderings of predictions, trained routing) and some study instruments are of an earlier
form of ISLA's inputs, the *nearest-token form*, and their captions name it.** The form has the reference configuration's
width, depth, slices and learning rate and the normalized slice reads. It differs from ISLA in how the boundary and the
prediction points enter the model, in its length unit and in its scales; @tbl-checkpoint-form lists the differences item
by item. The class refuses checkpoints of any other version (@sec-using-checkpoint), so these checkpoints are records of
the form, not models the class loads. A figure of the form that checkpoints of ISLA replace carries an In-flight callout
beside it.

| item | the nearest-token form | ISLA as Part II defines it |
|---|---|---|
| slice reads | the normalized slice reads | the normalized slice reads (@sec-isla-normalized-reads) |
| boundary conditions | one boundary schema shared by every condition: a labelled boundary is one mesh, its condition a one-hot label among each cell's fields | one boundary mesh per named condition, each with its own input layer and a learned offset, so a condition's identity is in the parameters; no label is read (@sec-isla-inputs) |
| boundary tokens | drawn by the datapipe before the forward call; the model reads the sample it is given | drawn inside the forward call from the full-resolution meshes: in proportion to measure, water-filled across the conditions, systematic along a space-filling order, each kept cell carrying its Horvitz–Thompson measure; a fixed start at evaluation |
| a prediction point's wall geometry | the distance and direction to the nearest *sampled* boundary token, signed by that token's normal | the exact closest point on the full-resolution boundary meshes, signed by the pseudo-normal, encoded continuously through the surface; the same for every draw of the boundary tokens (@sec-exact-geometry-draw) |
| stored signed distance | on AirfRANS, Tensile2d and the lug, the dataset's `sdf` and `sdf_normals` read as a prediction-point input | none read |
| length unit $L$ | the RMS pairwise distance of the boundary cells the model is given, each cell at its centroid; on the interior task, of the datapipe's sample | the RMS pairwise distance of the full-resolution boundary, computed before the draw, each cell with its own second moment: exact for the meshed boundary and the same for every draw (@sec-isla-frame) |
| scales | none declared; on AirfRANS the inlet direction and the raw inlet speed in m/s as a global scalar | the scales the AirfRANS and AeroZoo configurations declare, computed per case from the boundary and the global inputs; none declared elsewhere (@sec-using-scales) |

: The nearest-token form against ISLA as the class defines it. On a surface task the
prediction points are the boundary cells, so the last two rows do not arise there. How to read this: the rows are the
whole difference in what enters the model; the baselines' inputs are the same in both columns (@tbl-model-inputs). Sources:
the class, `physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/`; the form's checkpoints as the reduction of the geometry evidence describes them,
results/campaigns_2026-10-19/geo_evidence/geo_evidence.json (`doc`).
{#tbl-checkpoint-form}

Unless a caption says otherwise, the study runs of the next section are of the same form, with the raw slice reads.

## Study configurations {#sec-study-configurations}

**A study run on an ISLA other than the reference configuration has one tag in its caption: "Instrument: ISLA at
⟨width⟩ wide, ⟨slices⟩ slices, ⟨rate⟩, raw slice reads". Such a study is read for slopes and mechanisms, never as a
standing.** Several of the book's mechanism probes, sampling probes and scaling ladders were run on other
configurations of ISLA, most of them smaller. They used fewer slices, another width, another learning rate, and the
*raw slice reads*, the
ablation of @sec-isla-layer in which the slice sublayer pools and broadcasts the raw token state instead of its
LayerNorm. A slope (how an error moves with cells, data or width) and a mechanism (where a dependence on the sample lives)
carry over between configurations of one architecture. An absolute error does not, and no tagged number is compared with a
standing. A study whose runs used the *linear* routing score, an unbounded affine score in place of ISLA's bounded cosine
score, has the variant "Instrument: ISLA at ⟨width⟩ wide, ⟨slices⟩ slices, ⟨rate⟩, linear routing, raw slice reads".
@tbl-study-configurations lists the configurations as they appear in the book's artifacts.

| tag | layers | width | slices | learning rate | routing score | training cells | where the book uses it |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|---|---|
| ISLA at 384 wide, 256 slices, 5e-4, raw slice reads | 12 | 384 | 256 | $5 \times 10^{-4}$ | cosine | 200,000 | the biased-draw probe, the slice territories, the rotation-augmented comparison (@sec-contract-studies, @sec-pose-contract); the 384-wide points of the capacity ladders (@sec-capacity) |
| ISLA at 192 wide, 256 slices, 1e-3, linear routing, raw slice reads | 12 | 192 | 256 | $10^{-3}$ | linear | 100,000 (cars), 200,000 (wings) | the training-law swap (@sec-training-law) |
| ISLA at 512 wide, 512 slices, 3.75e-4, raw slice reads | 12 | 512 | 512 | $3.75 \times 10^{-4}$ | cosine | 200,000 | the study that swaps the nearest-token wall geometry for the exact one on the DrivAerML Volume task, an instrument of the nearest-token form (@sec-checkpoint-form) |
| ISLA at 768 wide, 256 slices, 2.5e-4, raw slice reads | 12 | 768 | 256 | $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ | cosine | 20,000 | the tie diagnostic on the lug (@sec-medial-ties) |
| capacity ladders | 12 to 48 | 192 to 1,536 | 256 | named per point | cosine or linear, named per point | 10,000 to 200,000, named per point | the scaling fits and the cells ladder (@sec-capacity); each point names its own configuration |

: The study configurations of ISLA and where the book uses them. Every configuration other than the reference one uses
the raw slice reads. *Learning rate*: the width rule $10^{-3} \times 192 / \text{width}$. *Routing score*: *cosine* is the bounded cosine score of ISLA's slice
routing (@sec-isla-slices); *linear* is an unbounded affine score of the token state, which the class does not have, and a
tag names it. How to read this: a caption that has a tag reads its numbers against other numbers with the same tag, never
against a standing. Sources: the training-run configurations recorded in
`results/campaigns_2026-10-02/char/rf1/rf1_isla_ref/metrics.jsonl` (384 wide, 256 slices, $5 \times 10^{-4}$) and
`cs/cs_t2dz_isla/metrics.jsonl` (768 wide, 256 slices, $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$); the protocol strings of
`results/consistency_r1_2026-09-23.json`, `results/trainarea_dr_r1_2026-09-23.json` and
`results/char/vol_geo_2026-10-05.json`. {#tbl-study-configurations}

Every figure and table caption in the book ends with the artifact in `results/` from which it is computed, and every figure
is drawn from that artifact when the page renders.
